en: The *Sūtra on Praising the Merits of the Saṃgha* is extracted in brief from the Āgamas. Extolling the great field of merit, the jewels of the Saṃgha,
Mahābrahmā and Śakra, with the voice of Great Brahmā, praised the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Just as the earth is firm, so too do the various deities and others praise the entire assembly of the Saṅgha-ratna;
I am an ordained person appearing in the age of the Final Dharma, a member of the eternally abiding Saṅgha-ratna, an eternally abiding monk.
The Sangha Jewel, together with the Sangha, promotes the Buddha-Dharma;
Aiming to seek the subtle and wondrous fruit of Bodhi, Within this turbid, suffering, and evil world, They always abide among the Tathāgata’s pure assembly.
Within the Saṃgha there may be those who seek the four fruits, or those who have realized the fruits while among the Saṃgha;
these eight classes of superior persons remain in harmonious union within the Saṃgha, never ceasing.
Some are dhūta practitioners who constantly beg for alms; some delight in the stillness of the mountain retreats;
and even regarding the most subtle precepts, they do not violate the Tathāgata’s solemn commands and teachings.
Some possess profound and vast learning and wisdom; some have stilled their thoughts and practiced the various dhyānas.
All gather together within the assembly of the Sangha, just as the hundred rivers flow back to the great ocean.

The Sangha of Great Virtue, supreme and wondrous jewels, who nurture the seeds of merit for all sentient beings and are able to bestow the excellent fruits upon gods and humans— none surpass the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
If one gives a single handful of water with a virtuous mind to the Saṃgha, the merit obtained exceeds the volume of the great ocean;
while even a mote of dust may yet be counted, the merit from giving jewels to the Saṃgha is inexhaustible.
If a person seeks seclusion in the future and wishes to cross the river of poverty within birth and death,
they should swiftly cultivate a sincere mind and plant the seeds of cause and effect within the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
In this most excellent and fertile field of merit, if there are those who plant the seeds of virtue,
they shall reap a harvest without bound in the future, just like the great rain held within the clouds.
The giver who does not calculate or measure, but offers with impartiality and a mind free of duality—
only such a person is capable of receiving the supreme fruit among gods and humans.

Adorned with immeasurable merit, the assembly of disciples of the World-Honored One of Great Compassion is difficult for ordinary people with their fleshly eyes to distinguish, like fire covered by ashes.
Some may outwardly manifest the appearance of violating the precepts, while inwardly they secretly possess immeasurable merits;
one should believe in, follow, and honor them, for the conduct of the wise and holy cannot be fathomed by ordinary fools.
Some may outwardly manifest the possession of dignified deportment, while others may show themselves as unable to renounce their desires;
though people observing these external signs call them ordinary folk, it does not preclude that they are, internally, sages.
Like four *āmra* fruits within, whose ripeness and rawness are difficult to distinguish and cannot be differentiated, so too it is with the disciples of the Tathāgata;
those who possess the precepts and those who lack them are likewise hard to discern.
Therefore, I earnestly exhort all people: do not listen to those who revile or abuse the Sangha Jewel.
If you wish not to sink into the ocean of suffering, you should always respect and honor it as one plants a fertile field.
Those who always desire to experience happiness among humans should likewise make offerings to the community of bhikṣus;
they should not, with the inferior mind of an ordinary person, discriminate among the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples.
If there are faithful men and women who, through ten recitations,
can give rise to a mind of faith and impartially make offerings to the community of bhikṣus, such persons shall obtain immeasurable retribution.
If one gives rise to wrong views regarding the Saṅgha, one will certainly fall into the three evil realms in the future;
the World-Honored One has personally proclaimed this with his Brahma-voice from his golden mouth—this is truly not false.
It would be better to have one's tongue cut by a sharp blade, or even to have one's body crushed by a pestle,
than to harbor a single thought of anger and malice to slander the Tathāgata and the pure Saṅgha.
It would be better to swallow a great red-hot iron ball, or for fierce flames to burst forth from one's mouth,
than to utter even a single word of frivolous debate to revile the pure assembly of those who have left the home life.

It would be better to cut and carve oneself with a sharp blade, to maim one's limbs and destroy one's flesh, than to mock and jest with the foolish; why then curse, strike, or revile the assembly of bhikṣus?
It would be better to pluck out both one's own eyes with one's own hands, or to suffer from congenital blindness for many kalpas,
than to look upon a person who practices the cultivation of detachment with an evil eye.
It would be better to destroy a vihāra or a caitya, or to burn a stūpa containing relics of the seven precious gems,
than to utter evil words among the Saṃgha or to slander the pure assembly of the Tathāgata.
One who destroys a stūpa falls by their own accord, Suffering various miseries for immeasurable kalpas;
Those who delight in speaking of the faults of the Saṃgha Fall themselves and lead immeasurable multitudes [to ruin].
Therefore, the wise should reflect well: do not give rise to contempt or arrogance toward the Saṅgha;
guard your own verbal karma against error, and do not speak of this person’s observance of precepts or that person’s violation of them.
If one slanders a śramaṇa with a single evil word, one shall fall into hell and undergo extreme suffering;
upon emerging from that hell and obtaining a human body, one will immediately receive the retribution of deafness, blindness, and muteness.
In this world there are many foolish and inferior people Who speak of the various faults and evils of monks and nuns;
Because of this, they fall into the evil realms, Sinking and drowning in the sea of suffering for eternal kalpas.
The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One pays homage to the great assembly; he reveres and honors the Sangha of Great Virtue in harmony.
Even the Buddhas themselves are diligent in this regard—how much more so should ordinary people refrain from treating the assembly with contempt?
In this world, there are many people of faith who revere the disciples of the World-Honored One;
yet when they hear the faults of the Triple Gem being discussed, they harbor resentment toward the Saṃgha and give rise to wrong views.
Therefore, they cause the virtuous to fall back and destroy the Tathāgata’s pure assembly;
they shall not behold the thousand World-Honored Ones of the Bhadrakalpa—for this reason, the wise should reflect upon it.
In the past, there was the bhikṣu Kokālika, who reviled the Saṃgha with a single evil word;
he fell into the Padma Hell, where his tongue was plowed into tens of thousands of pieces.
There were also disciples of Kāśyapa Buddha who slandered and reviled countless people of the world;
owing to this evil karma, they cast off their remaining physical forms and once again underwent the suffering of the Ploughed-Tongue Hell.
If a śramaṇa harbors anger and reviles others, he still incurs immeasurable retribution for his verbal karma;
how much more so for an unvirtuous layperson who, by reviling the Saṅgha, avoids falling into the evil realms?
Therefore, a wise person should not revile even grass, trees, bricks, or tiles,
much less disparage pure renunciants who practice the wholesome dharmas of detachment from desire.
Even if the fire of desire fiercely burns the heart and defiles the pure precepts of *śīla*,
one can soon and swiftly repent and eliminate them, thereby re-entering the ranks of the Tathāgata’s noble assembly.
Just as a person who has momentarily lost their way, Having eyes, can still find the original path;
So too, though a bhikṣu may violate the World-Honored One’s prohibitions, Though he has momentarily transgressed, he can still extinguish it.
Just as when a person stumbles on level ground, having feet they can still quickly rise;
though a bhikṣu may temporarily lack śīla, even if he commits an offense, he can soon restore it.
Just as a vessel made of gold or precious gems in this world remains of equal value even when broken,
whereas a wooden vessel, though perfectly intact and leak-proof, cannot be compared to that broken precious vessel.
Though a bhikṣu who has violated the prohibitions lacks precepts, The merit of one who first set out in the homeless life is superior;
Even hundreds of thousands of millions of laypeople, Though their merit be great, cannot equal his.
The ordained disciple is capable of bearing the task of succeeding to the Dharma of the Tathāgata in the final age;
though worldly people possess immeasurable myriad virtues, they cannot propagate the holy teaching for even a moment.
Even for a most lowly monk who has transgressed prohibitions and broken the precepts, making offerings to him still yields a reward of ten billion merits;
therefore, the World-Honored One praised this supreme cause, whereby one receives noble status among gods and humans.
Therefore, I earnestly exhort all people: do not disparage the Sangha, the Jewel of the Tathāgata.
Because of the causes and conditions of practicing evil in this life, when future karma is fulfilled, you too will disparage the Buddha.
Conditioned by these factors of body, speech, and mind, one forever severs the seeds of humanity and divinity;
one shall fall into the three miserable realms and sink for billions of kalpas without respite.
If one gives rise to right faith toward the pure assembly, there shall be no offense of slandering the Sangha;
always able to guard against the faults of verbal karma, one does not speak ill of the Tathāgata’s jewel-like assembly.
If a person has committed the offense of reviling the Saṃgha, they must with sincere resolve quickly seek repentance;
do not give rise to arrogance toward the Saṃgha, for you will surely regret it when suffering arises in a future life.
If the merit possessed by the Saṃgha in a single kṣaṇa cannot be contained even upon the great earth,
how much more so for those who, month after month and year after year, steadfastly uphold the Tathāgata’s strict prohibitions and precepts?
The Buddha could not exhaustively describe the retribution for this person’s merit of upholding the precepts even in a single kalpa;
how much less could ordinary worldly people know its limit? Such blessings are equal to empty space and are immeasurable.
One should know that the assembly of the Saṅgha-ratna of Śākyamuni Tathāgata is adorned with vast merit;
therefore, one must not permit laypeople to revile, insult, beat, or scold ordained monks.
Even if you see a śramaṇa violating the precepts, you should broaden your mind and not harbor resentment or contempt;
just as one enters a fragrant thicket to gather exquisite flowers, one should not pluck and select only the withered branches and leaves.
In the vast and pure ocean of the Buddha-dharma, there are many who uphold the precepts and practice with diligence;
even if among them some should violate the rules of decorum, laypeople should not give rise to slander.
Just as in a field there are newly sown crops, among which there may also be weeds such as barnyard grass and tares—
one should regard the fertile field with equal respect and should not engage in discrimination by selecting one over the other.
For this reason, the World-Honored One established rules for all people: do not permit the slandering of the assembly of śramaṇas;
one should only respect them and give rise to a heart of reverence, so that together they may receive the superior retribution of the various devas.
Though the Buddha-sun has long since set, the Sangha-treasure continues to radiate its brilliance, transmitting the lamp of the Dharma;
like a dragon king sending down sweet rain, it universally nourishes the sprouts of the great earth.

The Saṃgha Jewel is likewise: it rains down the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma rain, nourishing all living beings who are withered and thirsty, and causing the sprouts of goodness and the seeds of merit to grow.
Having planted roots of merit over many eons, they have become disciples of the Tathāgata;
dwelling within the ocean of the Dharma of the noble ones, they drink the wondrous nectar of liberation.
Upholding the teachings of the World-Honored One in the final age, Spreading transformation throughout the lands of the ten directions,
Benefiting all sentient beings, Ensuring that the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma never ceases.
When the Buddha-dharma has long since vanished and perished, The monasteries and viharas will be destroyed and turned into ruins;
The niches, stupas, and sacred images will all fall into desolation, And even if one wishes to make offerings, it will be difficult to do so.
Even the forms of monks depicted in murals cannot be seen; how much less can one hear the True Dharma?
A human body is difficult to obtain, yet having been born among humans, one has now encountered the Buddha-Dharma, which is so rarely met.
Why, in this wondrous and excellent field of merit, do you not plant the seeds of future virtue?
The path to the dark realms is remote and impassable; you must prepare your provisions for what lies ahead.
If one does not plant seeds within this excellent field of merit, it will serve as no provision for the perilous path to come;
therefore, all people should reflect well and bestow gifts upon the Sangha who have heard the Sūtras.
Relying on the sutras, I have briefly praised the Jewel of the Sangha; Its merit is immeasurable, pervading all of space.
I dedicate this to all living beings, Vowing that together we may meet Maitreya in the future.
